_description: Veterinary Nomenclature (VeNom) to SNOMED-CT crosswalk for the 14 One Health-relevant diseases in this dataset. VeNom is the de-facto controlled vocabulary for small-animal practice, maintained by the VeNom Coding Group at the Royal Veterinary College (UK). SNOMED-CT is the human-medicine standard. A reliable crosswalk is required for any system that surfaces cross-species clinical signals across human and veterinary EHRs.
_source_notes: Source for VeNom codes: VeNom Coding Group (venomcoding.org), v3.x ontology browser; manually checked.
Source for SNOMED-CT codes: SNOMED International browser; veterinary content is sparse in SNOMED-CT, so we fall back to the closest human-disease concept where a vet-specific child does not exist.
Coverage limitations stated explicitly per disease — this crosswalk is incomplete by design (production builds extend it through a curated review process with veterinary informaticians).

tier_definitions.exact: VeNom term has a direct SNOMED-CT equivalent at the same level of specificity (rare).
tier_definitions.close: VeNom term maps to a SNOMED-CT concept that is broader by one or two levels; clinically equivalent for surveillance.
tier_definitions.approximated: VeNom and SNOMED-CT have related concepts but the mapping requires editorial judgment (e.g., species-specific manifestation). Suitable for cluster detection but not for granular reporting.
tier_definitions.no_mapping: No SNOMED-CT concept exists for the VeNom term; vet-side surveillance can still capture the case but cross-species linkage is degraded.

_crosswalk_quality._caveat: VeNom-to-SNOMED-CT mapping is a known active research problem in veterinary informatics. The HL7 Veterinary Care Workgroup (FHIR R5-vet-ballot) is the closest standardization effort. We document our editorial choices below; a production deployment would route ambiguous cases through a vet-informaticist review queue before publication.

mappings.editorial_notes: Same fungal pathogen across species; clinical presentation differs (canine bone involvement is common; equine pulmonary is dominant). Cluster-level surveillance treats them as the same condition for One Health purposes.
Canine reservoir is the medically important sentinel. Cats rarely show clinical RMSF. Brown dog tick (Rhipicephalus sanguineus) cycle is the AZ-specific transmission route.

Feline plague is the human-relevant sentinel — cats develop pneumonic plague that can transmit to humans via respiratory droplets. SNOMED-CT lacks species-specific child concepts, so we use the parent. Northern AZ (Coconino, Apache, Navajo) is the enzootic zone.

snomed_ct.display: Disease caused by West Nile virus

mappings.editorial_notes: Horses are dead-end hosts but clinically tractable sentinels with reportable case definitions. Avian die-offs (especially corvids) are the upstream sentinel signal that ADHS tracks.

venom.display: Hantavirus (no clinical disease in companion animals)

mappings.editorial_notes: Deer mice (Peromyscus maniculatus) are asymptomatic carriers and are not seen in companion-animal practice — surveillance is via household rodent observation rather than clinical diagnosis. The 'sentinel' for HPS is environmental (rodent presence) more than veterinary.
Canine ehrlichiosis is the dominant veterinary form; brown dog tick is the shared vector with RMSF. Often co-detected with RMSF in households.
Canine leptospirosis is a sentinel for shared-water-source exposure. Cattle leptospirosis carries a production-loss signal (abortion, drop in milk) that ADA tracks separately.

The veterinary presentation is reproductive (abortion storm) — dramatically different from human Q fever's atypical pneumonia presentation. SNOMED-CT does not have a 'caprine abortion due to Coxiella' child concept; we use the parent. AZ ranches in Cochise and Apache counties are the highest-risk premises.
Veterinary nomenclature uses 'avian chlamydiosis' for the same organism (Chlamydia psittaci). SNOMED-CT human-side 'Psittacosis' covers the human disease. Mapping is editorial.

Outdoor cats with classic ulceroglandular tularemia are the primary clinical sentinel for hunter or rabbit-handler exposure in the household. Rabbit die-offs (less commonly seen in practice) are the upstream environmental sentinel.

Same pathogen and clinical entity across species; reporting requirements differ (USDA federal reportable for animals, ADHS reportable for humans, both require 24-hour notification). PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) workflow on the human side is gated by the animal diagnosis.

Reptile and poultry shedding is asymptomatic but is the sentinel for human exposure risk. Backyard-poultry households have a documented 30-fold elevated salmonellosis risk. Surveillance is via household-pet inventory rather than per-encounter veterinary diagnosis.
Bovine TB in dairy herds is the leading sentinel for human zoonotic-TB cases via unpasteurized dairy. AZ-Mexico border dairy trade is the highest-risk pathway; ADA actively surveils.
Caprine and bovine abortion clusters are the leading sentinel. Border-county (Santa Cruz, Cochise, Yuma) trade in unpasteurized goat-milk products is a recurrent source for human cases.
